question: The first compound is an organic molecule with the formula HO₂CCO(CH₂)₂CO₂H; it appears as a white, nontoxic solid and is a common dicarboxylic acid that, in physiological pH, exists mainly as its conjugate base α‑ketoglutarate and is classified as a 2‑ketocarboxylic acid (its β‑isomer is β‑ketoglutaric acid). The second compound is a waste product generated from the breakdown of creatine phosphate in muscle; its name derives from the ancient Greek word for “flesh,” and it is released into the bloodstream at a roughly constant rate that scales with an individual’s muscle mass. Using reliable chemical databases, calculate the difference in molecular weight (g·mol⁻¹) between the first compound and the second compound. Provide the absolute value of this difference.

entity_document.title: Creatinine
entity_document.text:
<<A_RELEVANT>>Creatinine (/kriˈætɪnɪn, -ˌniːn/; from Ancient Greek  κρέας (kréas) 'flesh') is a breakdown product of creatine phosphate from muscle and protein metabolism.<</A_RELEVANT>> It is released at a constant rate by the body (depending on muscle mass).[3][4]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Serum creatinine (a blood measurement) is an important indicator of kidney function, because it is an easily measured byproduct of muscle metabolism that is excreted unchanged by the kidneys.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Creatinine itself is produced via a biological system involving creatine, phosphocreatine (also known as creatine phosphate), and adenosine triphosphate (ATP, the body's immediate energy supply).[5]<</A_RELEVANT>>

Creatine is synthesized primarily in the liver by methylation of glycocyamine (guanidino acetate, synthesized in the kidney from the amino acids arginine and glycine) by S-adenosyl methionine. <<A_RELEVANT>>It is then transported in the blood to other organs, muscles, and the brain, where it is phosphorylated to phosphocreatine, a high-energy compound.[6] Creatine conversion to phosphocreatine is catalysed by creatine kinase; spontaneous formation of creatinine occurs during the reaction.[7]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Creatinine is removed from the blood chiefly by the kidneys, primarily by glomerular filtration, but also by proximal tubular secretion.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Little or no tubular reabsorption of creatinine occurs.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>If filtration in the kidney is deficient, blood creatinine concentrations rise.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Therefore, creatinine concentrations in blood and urine may be used to calculate the creatinine clearance (CrCl), which correlates approximately with the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Blood creatinine concentrations may also be used alone to estimate the GFR (eGFR).<</A_RELEVANT>>

The GFR is clinically important as a measurement of kidney function. <<A_RELEVANT>>However, in cases of severe kidney dysfunction the CrCl rate will overestimate the GFR, because hypersecretion of creatinine by the proximal renal tubules will account for a larger fraction of the total creatinine cleared.[8] Ketoacids, cimetidine, and trimethoprim reduce creatinine tubular secretion and therefore increase the accuracy of the GFR estimate, in particular in severe kidney dysfunction. (In the absence of secretion, creatinine behaves like inulin.)[9][10]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>An alternative estimation of kidney function can be made when interpreting the blood plasma concentration of creatinine along with that of urea.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>BUN-to-creatinine ratio (the ratio of blood urea nitrogen to creatinine) can indicate other problems besides those intrinsic to the kidney; for example, a urea concentration raised out of proportion to the creatinine may indicate a prerenal problem, such as volume depletion.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Counterintuitively, supporting the observation of higher creatinine production in women than in men, and putting into question the algorithms for GFR that do not distinguish for sex, women have higher muscle protein synthesis and higher muscle protein turnover across their life span.[11] As HDL supports muscle anabolism, higher muscle protein turnover links increased creatine to the generally higher serum HDL in women compared with serum HDL in men.[12][13]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Studies suggest that creatinine can be effective in killing bacteria of many species, both Gram positive and Gram negative, as well as diverse antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains.[14] Creatinine appears not to affect the growth of fungi and yeasts; this can be used to isolate slower growing fungi free from the normal bacterial populations found in most environmental samples.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The mechanism by which creatinine kills bacteria is not currently known.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Some reports also suggest that creatinine may have immunosuppressive properties.[15][16]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Serum creatinine is the most commonly used indicator (although not a direct measure) of renal function.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>A raised creatinine is not always representative of a true reduction in GFR.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>A high reading may be due to: increased production of creatinine (with no association to reduced kidney function), interference with the assay, or reduced tubular secretion of creatinine.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>An increase in serum creatinine can be due to increased ingestion of cooked meat (which contains creatinine converted from creatine by the heat from cooking) or excessive intake of protein and creatine supplements, taken to enhance athletic performance.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Intense exercise can increase creatinine by increasing muscle breakdown.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Hypovolaemia of any cause, may have an associated increase in creatinine concentration, secondary to the expected reduction in GFR.<</A_RELEVANT>> This is pre-renal impairment of kidney function. Several medications and chromogens can interfere with the chemical assay. <<A_RELEVANT>>Creatinine secretion by the renal tubules can be blocked by some medications, again increasing measured creatinine.[17]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Diagnostic serum creatinine studies are used to determine renal function.[4] The reference interval is 0.6–1.3 mg/dL (53–115 μmol/L).[4] It is simple to measure serum creatinine, and it is the most commonly used indicator of renal function.[6]<</A_RELEVANT>>

question: The first compound is a naturally occurring organic molecule that contains a sulfonic acid group rather than a carboxylic acid, is not incorporated into proteins, and was first isolated from ox bile in the early 19th century. The second compound is an amino acid stereoisomer that is present in humans, is also produced by a common gram‑negative bacterium, and belongs to the species Homo sapiens. Using a reliable chemical database, determine the difference in total hydrogen‑bond capacity (the sum of hydrogen‑bond donors and acceptors) between the first compound and the second compound. Express the answer as a positive integer (first minus second).

entity_document.title: Taurine
entity_document.text:
<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine (/ˈtɔːriːn/ ⓘ;[1] IUPAC: 2-aminoethanesulfonic acid[2]) is a naturally occurring organic compound with the chemical formula H2N−CH2−CH2−SO2−OH in its non-zwitterionic form and H3N+−CH2−CH2−SO−3 in its zwitterionic form, and is a non-proteinogenic amino sulfonic acid widely distributed in mammalian tissues and organs.[2][3] Structurally, by containing a sulfonic acid group instead of a carboxylic acid group, it is not involved in protein synthesis but is still usually referred to as an amino acid.[2][4][5][6] As non-proteinogenic amino sulfonic acid, it is not encoded by the genetic code and is distinguished from the protein-building α-amino acids.[7]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is an ingredient in some energy drinks in amounts of 1–3 grams per serving.[11][42]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is now a requirement of the Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO) and any dry or wet food product labeled approved by the AAFCO should have a minimum of 0.1% taurine in dry food and 0.2% in wet food.[51] Studies suggest the amino acid should be supplied at 10 mg/kg of bodyweight per day for domestic cats.[52]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine appears to be essential for the development of passerine birds.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Many passerines seek out taurine-rich spiders to feed their young, particularly just after hatching.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Researchers compared the behaviours and development of birds fed a taurine-supplemented diet to a control diet and found the juveniles fed taurine-rich diets as neonates were much larger risk takers and more adept at spatial learning tasks.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Under natural conditions, each blue tit nestling receive 1 mg of taurine per day from parents.[54]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is a major constituent of bile and can be found in the large intestine.<</A_RELEVANT>> It is named after Latin taurus, meaning bull or ox, as it was first isolated from ox bile in 1827 by German scientists Friedrich Tiedemann and Leopold Gmelin.

<<A_RELEVANT>>Although taurine is abundant in human organs, it is not an essential human dietary nutrient and is not included among nutrients with a recommended intake level.[8] Among the diverse pathways by which natural taurine can be biosynthesized, its human pathways (primarily in the human liver) are from cysteine and/or methionine.[9][10]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is commonly sold as a dietary supplement.[11] Taurine is used as a food additive to meet essential dietary intake levels for cats,[12] and supplemental dietary support for dogs and poultry.[13]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine was first isolated from ox bile in 1827 by German scientists Friedrich Tiedemann and Leopold Gmelin.[14][15] Another German scientist Von H.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Demarcay first used its common chemical name Taurine in 1838, derived from the Latin taurus (cognate to Ancient Greek  ταῦρος, taûros) meaning bull or ox.[16][17][15] It was subsequently identified in human bile in 1846 by Edmund Ronalds.[18][better source needed]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is widely distributed in nature, particularly in animal tissues.[3][better source needed] Moreover, it is abundant in nature, including in animal organs,[19][better source needed]  and further, as substrates in the biosynthesis of bile salts.[9] Taurine concentrations in human cells may derive from at least three processes:<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>It is not an essential human dietary nutrient, resulting in the absence of taurine from compounds having a Reference Daily Intake.[8]  Its role in human physiology is unknown.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is a major constituent of bile, and can be found in the large intestine.[21] Its concentrations in land plants are low or undetectable, but up to a substantial wet weight has been found in algae.[22][23]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine exists as a zwitterion H3N+CH2CH2SO−3, as verified by X-ray crystallography.[24] The sulfonic acid has a low pKa[25] ensuring that it is fully ionized to the sulfonate at the pHs found in the intestinal tract.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Among the diverse pathways by which natural taurine can be biosynthesized, its pathways in the human liver are from cysteine and/or methionine.[9][10] With regard to the route from cysteine: mammalian taurine synthesis occurs in the liver via the cysteine sulfinic acid pathway.<</A_RELEVANT>> In this pathway, cysteine is first oxidized to its sulfinic acid, catalyzed by the enzyme cysteine dioxygenase. <<A_RELEVANT>>Cysteine sulfinic acid, in turn, is decarboxylated by sulfinoalanine decarboxylase to form hypotaurine.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Hypotaurine is enzymatically oxidized to yield taurine by hypotaurine dehydrogenase.[26]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is also produced by the transsulfuration pathway, which converts homocysteine into cystathionine.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The cystathionine is then converted to hypotaurine by the sequential action of three enzymes: cystathionine gamma-lyase, cysteine dioxygenase, and cysteine sulfinic acid decarboxylase.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Hypotaurine is then oxidized to taurine as described above.[27]<</A_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Taurine
property_documents.document:
<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine (/ˈtɔːriːn/ ⓘ;[1] IUPAC: 2-aminoethanesulfonic acid[2]) is a naturally occurring organic compound with the chemical formula H2N−CH2−CH2−SO2−OH in its non-zwitterionic form and H3N+−CH2−CH2−SO−3 in its zwitterionic form, and is a non-proteinogenic amino sulfonic acid widely distributed in mammalian tissues and organs.[2][3] Structurally, by containing a sulfonic acid group instead of a carboxylic acid group, it is not involved in protein synthesis but is still usually referred to as an amino acid.[2][4][5][6] As non-proteinogenic amino sulfonic acid, it is not encoded by the genetic code and is distinguished from the protein-building α-amino acids.[7]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is an ingredient in some energy drinks in amounts of 1–3 grams per serving.[11][42]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is now a requirement of the Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO) and any dry or wet food product labeled approved by the AAFCO should have a minimum of 0.1% taurine in dry food and 0.2% in wet food.[51] Studies suggest the amino acid should be supplied at 10 mg/kg of bodyweight per day for domestic cats.[52]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine appears to be essential for the development of passerine birds.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Many passerines seek out taurine-rich spiders to feed their young, particularly just after hatching.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Researchers compared the behaviours and development of birds fed a taurine-supplemented diet to a control diet and found the juveniles fed taurine-rich diets as neonates were much larger risk takers and more adept at spatial learning tasks.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Under natural conditions, each blue tit nestling receive 1 mg of taurine per day from parents.[54]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is a major constituent of bile and can be found in the large intestine.<</A_RELEVANT>> It is named after Latin taurus, meaning bull or ox, as it was first isolated from ox bile in 1827 by German scientists Friedrich Tiedemann and Leopold Gmelin.

<<A_RELEVANT>>Although taurine is abundant in human organs, it is not an essential human dietary nutrient and is not included among nutrients with a recommended intake level.[8] Among the diverse pathways by which natural taurine can be biosynthesized, its human pathways (primarily in the human liver) are from cysteine and/or methionine.[9][10]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is commonly sold as a dietary supplement.[11] Taurine is used as a food additive to meet essential dietary intake levels for cats,[12] and supplemental dietary support for dogs and poultry.[13]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine was first isolated from ox bile in 1827 by German scientists Friedrich Tiedemann and Leopold Gmelin.[14][15] Another German scientist Von H.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Demarcay first used its common chemical name Taurine in 1838, derived from the Latin taurus (cognate to Ancient Greek  ταῦρος, taûros) meaning bull or ox.[16][17][15] It was subsequently identified in human bile in 1846 by Edmund Ronalds.[18][better source needed]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Taurine is widely distributed in nature, particularly in animal tissues.[3][better source needed] Moreover, it is abundant in nature, including in animal organs,[19][better source needed]  and further, as substrates in the biosynthesis of bile salts.[9] Taurine concentrations in human cells may derive from at least three processes:<</A_RELEVANT>>

question: The first steroid hormone is the principal mineralocorticoid produced by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex and is essential for sodium conservation in the kidney, salivary glands, sweat glands, and colon, while also regulating blood pressure, plasma sodium, and potassium levels through mineralocorticoid receptors in the distal tubules and collecting ducts. The second steroid hormone is a 21‑carbon corticosteroid synthesized in the adrenal cortex that becomes the predominant glucocorticoid when cortisol synthesis is blocked in 17α‑hydroxylase deficiency. Using a reliable chemical database, determine the total number of hydrogen‑bond donors and acceptors for each compound and calculate the difference in their combined H‑bond capacity (donors + acceptors) between the first and the second compound.

entity_document.title: Aldosterone
entity_document.text:
<<A_RELEVANT>>Aldosterone is the main mineralocorticoid steroid hormone produced by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex in the adrenal gland.[4][5] It is essential for sodium conservation in the kidney, salivary glands, sweat glands, and colon.[6]  It plays a central role in the homeostatic regulation of blood pressure, plasma sodium (Na+), and potassium (K+) levels.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>It does so primarily by acting on the mineralocorticoid receptors in the distal tubules and collecting ducts of the nephron.[6] It influences the reabsorption of sodium and excretion of potassium (from and into the tubular fluids, respectively) of the kidney, thereby indirectly influencing water retention or loss, blood pressure, and blood volume.[7] When dysregulated, aldosterone is pathogenic and contributes to the development and progression of cardiovascular and kidney disease.[8] Aldosterone has exactly the opposite function of the atrial natriuretic hormone secreted by the heart.[7]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Aldosterone is part of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>It has a plasma half-life of less than 20 minutes.[9] Drugs that interfere with the secretion or action of aldosterone are in use as antihypertensives, like lisinopril, which lowers blood pressure by blocking the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), leading to lower aldosterone secretion.<</A_RELEVANT>> The net effect of these drugs is to reduce sodium and water retention but increase the retention of potassium. In other words, these drugs stimulate the excretion of sodium and water in urine, while they block the excretion of potassium.

<<A_RELEVANT>>Another example is spironolactone, a potassium-sparing diuretic of the steroidal spirolactone group, which interferes with the aldosterone receptor (among others) leading to lower blood pressure by the mechanism described above.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Aldosterone was first isolated by Sylvia Tait (Simpson) and Jim Tait in 1953; in collaboration with Tadeusz Reichstein.[10][11][12]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Aldosterone and corticosterone share the first part of their biosynthetic pathways.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The last parts are mediated either by the aldosterone synthase (for aldosterone) or by the 11β-hydroxylase (for corticosterone).<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>These enzymes are nearly identical (they share 11β-hydroxylation and 18-hydroxylation functions), but aldosterone synthase is also able to perform an 18-oxidation.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Moreover, aldosterone synthase is found within the zona glomerulosa at the outer edge of the adrenal cortex; 11β-hydroxylase is found in the zona glomerulosa and zona fasciculata.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Aldosterone synthase is normally absent in other sections of the adrenal gland.[14]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The secretion of aldosterone has a diurnal rhythm.[16]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Aldosterone is the primary of several endogenous members of the class of mineralocorticoids in humans.[citation needed] Deoxycorticosterone is another important member of this class.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Aldosterone tends to promote Na+ and water retention, and lower plasma K+ concentration by the following mechanisms:<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Aldosterone is responsible for the reabsorption of about 2% of filtered sodium in the kidneys, which is nearly equal to the entire sodium content in human blood under normal glomerular filtration rates.[19]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Aldosterone, probably acting through mineralocorticoid receptors, may positively influence neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus.[20]<</A_RELEVANT>>

Steroid receptors are intracellular since steroid hormones are able to cross the cell membrane without a specific transporter. <<A_RELEVANT>>The aldosterone mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) complex binds on the DNA to specific hormone response element, which leads to gene specific transcription.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The MR is stimulated by both aldosterone and cortisol, but a mechanism protects the body from excess aldosterone receptor stimulation by glucocorticoids (such as cortisol), which happen to be present at much higher concentrations than mineralocorticoids in the healthy individual.<</A_RELEVANT>> The mechanism consists of an enzyme called 11β-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD). This enzyme co-localizes with intracellular adrenal steroid receptors and converts cortisol into cortisone, a relatively inactive metabolite with little affinity for the MR. Liquorice, which contains glycyrrhetinic acid, can inhibit 11β-HSD and lead to a mineralocorticoid excess syndrome.

<<A_RELEVANT>>Angiotensin is involved in regulating aldosterone and is the core regulation.[22] Angiotensin II acts synergistically with potassium, and the potassium feedback is virtually inoperative when no angiotensin II is present.[23] A small portion of the regulation resulting from angiotensin II must take place indirectly from decreased blood flow through the liver due to constriction of capillaries.[24] When the blood flow decreases so does the destruction of aldosterone by liver enzymes.<</A_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Corticosterone
property_documents.document:
<<A_RELEVANT>>Corticosterone, also known as 17-deoxycortisol and 11β,21-dihydroxyprogesterone,[1] is a 21-carbon steroid hormone of the corticosteroid type produced in the cortex of the adrenal glands.<</A_RELEVANT>> In the very rare case of congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 17α-hydroxylase deficiency cortisol production is blocked.[2]

<<A_RELEVANT>>With respect to recognition and long term memories, corticosterone has variable effects.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Studies show that the modification of certain chemical and brain processes that affect corticosterone levels can also impact stress effects on memory.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>In studies on rats, the fluctuations of corticosterone concentration are shown to prevent stress' impairment of recognition memory in lower amounts.<</A_RELEVANT>> These lower levels seem to be linked to the rescue of stress-induced attenuation of CA1 long-term potentiation.[13] When researchers looked at stress effects on LTM, they found many outcomes. <<A_RELEVANT>>In multiple studies, the formation of LTM (tested 24 h later) was found to be enhanced by corticosterone in some studies, while the persistence of LTM (tested at least 1 wk later) was only assisted by corticosterone in the late phase of memory consolidation and reconsolidation.[14][15] Stress facilitates the consolidation but disrupts the reconsolidation of emotional memory.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>As mentioned previously, the persistence of LTM is selectively enhanced when stress and corticosterone are administered during the late phase after acquisition, but it is disrupted when stress and corticosterone are administered during the late phase after retrieval of memory.[15] With regards to the persistence of LTM, there is a restricted time window between acquisition and retrieval where persistence is affected.<</A_RELEVANT>> These studies found that while persistence of LTM is selectively affected based on stage of memory, the formation of LTM is left intact after a certain length of time. <<A_RELEVANT>>Up to this point, studies have not agreed as to whether or not these processes are dependent on corticosterone or what even happens based on corticosterone in these processes and how memory is ultimately affected[citation needed].<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>In many species, including amphibians, reptiles, rodents and birds, corticosterone is a main glucocorticoid,[3] involved in regulation of energy, immune reactions, and stress responses.[4]<</A_RELEVANT>>

However, in humans, cortisol is the primary glucocorticoid that is produced primarily in the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex. <<A_RELEVANT>>Corticosterone has only weak glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid potencies in humans and is important mainly as an intermediate in the steroidogenic pathway from pregnenolone to aldosterone.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Corticosterone is converted to aldosterone by aldosterone synthase, found only in the mitochondria of glomerulosa cells.<</A_RELEVANT>> Glomerulosa cells are found in the zona glomerulosa, which is the most superficial region of endocrine cells in the adrenal cortex.[citation needed]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Corticosterone is the precursor molecule to the mineralocorticoid aldosterone, one of the major homeostatic modulators of sodium and potassium levels in vivo.[citation needed]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>One example of a release pathway relates to UV-B stimulation on the skins of certain amphibians such as the Rough-skinned Newt, Taricha granulosa; this trigger seems to cause the internal generation of corticosterone in that species.[5]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>A sizable amount of research has been done on the effects of corticosterone in birds.<</A_RELEVANT>> A brief survey of this research is below.

<<A_RELEVANT>>Corticosterone both inhibits protein synthesis and degrades proteins.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Birds with increased levels of corticosterone will have slower feather growth during their molting period and an extended period of poor flight.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>As a result, many birds have reduced levels of corticosterone when they moult so as to prevent the degradation of their new feathers.[6] Interestingly, higher levels of corticosterone are also associated with a wider range of exploration, despite beforementioned inhibited feather growth.[7]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Corticosterone has further developmental effects on birds.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Increased levels of corticosterone in chicks leads to increased begging for food and aggressiveness.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>In the short term this leads to higher chance of obtaining food, but in the long term, increased corticosterone in early life compromises the birds cognitive functioning (problem solving, association of visual cue with food, etc.).[8]<</A_RELEVANT>>

Parental response to increased begging by chicks is an increased time foraging for food. <<A_RELEVANT>>This leaves the nest of chicks without protection for increased durations of time.[9] To counter this, during extended periods of food shortage, chicks of some species may suppress corticosterone activity and thus reduce the negative effects elevated corticosterone induces.[10]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Corticosterone has multiple effects on memory.<</A_RELEVANT>> The main effects are seen through the impact of stress on emotional memories as well as long term memory (LTM).[citation needed]

question: The first protein is a type III intermediate filament that is named after a Latin word for flexible rods, is encoded by the VIM gene, and is a major component of the cytoskeleton in mesenchymal cells. The second protein is a muscle‑specific, type III intermediate filament encoded by the DES gene that links the sarcolemma, Z‑disk, and nuclear membrane to regulate sarcomere architecture. Using a reliable protein database, determine the amino‑acid sequence length of each protein and calculate how many times longer the sequence of the second protein is compared to the first. Express your answer as a dimensionless ratio rounded to four decimal places.

entity_document.title: Vimentin
entity_document.text:
<<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin is a structural protein that in humans is encoded by the VIM gene.<</A_RELEVANT>> Its name comes from the Latin vimentum, meaning an osier, withy (array of flexible rods).[5]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin is a type III intermediate filament (IF) protein that is expressed in mesenchymal cells.<</A_RELEVANT>> IF proteins are found in all animal cells[6] as well as bacteria.[7] Intermediate filaments, along with tubulin-based microtubules and actin-based microfilaments, comprise the cytoskeleton. <<A_RELEVANT>>All IF proteins are expressed in a highly developmentally-regulated fashion; vimentin is the major cytoskeletal component of mesenchymal cells.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Because of this, vimentin is often used as a marker of mesenchymally-derived cells or cells undergoing an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) during both normal development and metastatic progression.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The assembly of the fibrous vimentin filament that forms the cytoskeleton follows a gradual sequence.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The vimentin monomer has a central α-helical domain, capped on each end by non-helical amino (head) and carboxyl (tail) domains.[8] Two monomers are likely co-translationally expressed in a way that facilitates their interaction forming a coiled-coil dimer, which is the basic subunit of vimentin assembly.[9] A pair of coiled-coil dimers connect in an antiparallel fashion to form a tetramer.<</A_RELEVANT>> Eight tetramers join to form what is known as the unit-length filament (ULF), ULFs then stick to each other and elongate followed by compaction to form the fibrous proteins.[10]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin plays a significant role in supporting and anchoring the position of the organelles in the cytosol.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin is attached to the nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria, either laterally or terminally.[11]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The dynamic nature of vimentin is important when offering flexibility to the cell.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Scientists found that vimentin provided cells with a resilience absent from the microtubule or actin filament networks, when under mechanical stress in vivo.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Therefore, in general, it is accepted that vimentin is the cytoskeletal component responsible for maintaining cell integrity. (It was found that cells without vimentin are extremely delicate when disturbed with a micropuncture).[12] Transgenic mice that lack vimentin appeared normal and did not show functional differences.[13] It is possible that the microtubule network may have compensated for the absence of the intermediate network.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>This result supports an intimate interaction between microtubules and vimentin.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Moreover, when microtubule depolymerizers were present, vimentin reorganization occurred, once again implying a relationship between the two systems.[12] On the other hand, wounded mice that lack the vimentin gene heal slower than their wild type counterparts.[14]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>In essence, vimentin is responsible for maintaining cell shape, integrity of the cytoplasm, and stabilizing cytoskeletal interactions.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin has been shown to eliminate toxic proteins in JUNQ and IPOD inclusion bodies in asymmetric division of mammalian cell lines.[15]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Also, vimentin is found to control the transport of low-density lipoprotein, LDL, -derived cholesterol from a lysosome to the site of esterification.[16] With the blocking of transport of LDL-derived cholesterol inside the cell, cells were found to store a much lower percentage of the lipoprotein than normal cells with vimentin.<</A_RELEVANT>> This dependence seems to be the first process of a biochemical function in any cell that depends on a cellular intermediate filament network. This type of dependence has ramifications on the adrenal cells, which rely on cholesteryl esters derived from LDL.[16]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin plays a role in aggresome formation, where it forms a cage surrounding a core of aggregated protein.[17]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>In addition to its conventional intracellular localisation, vimentin can be found extracellularly.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin can be expressed as a cell surface protein and have suggested roles in immune reactions.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>It can also be released in phosphorylated forms to the extracellular space by activated macrophages, astrocytes are also known to release vimentin.[18]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>It has been used as a sarcoma tumor marker to identify mesenchyme, though its specificity as a bio marker has been disputed.[19][20][21] Vimentin is present in spindle cell squameous cell carcinoma.[22][23]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Methylation of the vimentin gene has been established as a biomarker of colon cancer and this is being utilized in the development of fecal tests for colon cancer.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Statistically significant levels of vimentin gene methylation have also been observed in certain upper gastrointestinal pathologies such as Barrett's esophagus, esophageal adenocarcinoma, and intestinal type gastric cancer.[24] High levels of DNA methylation in the promoter region have also been associated with markedly decreased survival in hormone positive breast cancers.[25]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Downregulation of vimentin was identified in cystic variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma using a proteomic approach.[26]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin is a type III intermediate filament (IF) protein that is expressed in mesenchymal cells.<</A_RELEVANT>> IF proteins are found in all animal cells[6] as well as bacteria.[7] Intermediate filaments, along with tubulin-based microtubules and actin-based microfilaments, comprise the cytoskeleton. <<A_RELEVANT>>All IF proteins are expressed in a highly developmentally-regulated fashion; vimentin is the major cytoskeletal component of mesenchymal cells.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Because of this, vimentin is often used as a marker of mesenchymally-derived cells or cells undergoing an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) during both normal development and metastatic progression.<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The assembly of the fibrous vimentin filament that forms the cytoskeleton follows a gradual sequence.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The vimentin monomer has a central α-helical domain, capped on each end by non-helical amino (head) and carboxyl (tail) domains.[8] Two monomers are likely co-translationally expressed in a way that facilitates their interaction forming a coiled-coil dimer, which is the basic subunit of vimentin assembly.[9] A pair of coiled-coil dimers connect in an antiparallel fashion to form a tetramer.<</A_RELEVANT>> Eight tetramers join to form what is known as the unit-length filament (ULF), ULFs then stick to each other and elongate followed by compaction to form the fibrous proteins.[10]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin plays a significant role in supporting and anchoring the position of the organelles in the cytosol.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin is attached to the nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria, either laterally or terminally.[11]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>The dynamic nature of vimentin is important when offering flexibility to the cell.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Scientists found that vimentin provided cells with a resilience absent from the microtubule or actin filament networks, when under mechanical stress in vivo.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Therefore, in general, it is accepted that vimentin is the cytoskeletal component responsible for maintaining cell integrity. (It was found that cells without vimentin are extremely delicate when disturbed with a micropuncture).[12] Transgenic mice that lack vimentin appeared normal and did not show functional differences.[13] It is possible that the microtubule network may have compensated for the absence of the intermediate network.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>This result supports an intimate interaction between microtubules and vimentin.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Moreover, when microtubule depolymerizers were present, vimentin reorganization occurred, once again implying a relationship between the two systems.[12] On the other hand, wounded mice that lack the vimentin gene heal slower than their wild type counterparts.[14]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>In essence, vimentin is responsible for maintaining cell shape, integrity of the cytoplasm, and stabilizing cytoskeletal interactions.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin has been shown to eliminate toxic proteins in JUNQ and IPOD inclusion bodies in asymmetric division of mammalian cell lines.[15]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Also, vimentin is found to control the transport of low-density lipoprotein, LDL, -derived cholesterol from a lysosome to the site of esterification.[16] With the blocking of transport of LDL-derived cholesterol inside the cell, cells were found to store a much lower percentage of the lipoprotein than normal cells with vimentin.<</A_RELEVANT>> This dependence seems to be the first process of a biochemical function in any cell that depends on a cellular intermediate filament network. This type of dependence has ramifications on the adrenal cells, which rely on cholesteryl esters derived from LDL.[16]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin plays a role in aggresome formation, where it forms a cage surrounding a core of aggregated protein.[17]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>In addition to its conventional intracellular localisation, vimentin can be found extracellularly.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Vimentin can be expressed as a cell surface protein and have suggested roles in immune reactions.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>It can also be released in phosphorylated forms to the extracellular space by activated macrophages, astrocytes are also known to release vimentin.[18]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>It has been used as a sarcoma tumor marker to identify mesenchyme, though its specificity as a bio marker has been disputed.[19][20][21] Vimentin is present in spindle cell squameous cell carcinoma.[22][23]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Methylation of the vimentin gene has been established as a biomarker of colon cancer and this is being utilized in the development of fecal tests for colon cancer.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Statistically significant levels of vimentin gene methylation have also been observed in certain upper gastrointestinal pathologies such as Barrett's esophagus, esophageal adenocarcinoma, and intestinal type gastric cancer.[24] High levels of DNA methylation in the promoter region have also been associated with markedly decreased survival in hormone positive breast cancers.[25]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Downregulation of vimentin was identified in cystic variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma using a proteomic approach.[26]<</A_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Desmin
property_documents.document:
<<A_RELEVANT>>Desmin is a protein that in humans is encoded by the DES gene.[5][6] Desmin is a muscle-specific, type III intermediate filament[7] that integrates the sarcolemma, Z disk, and nuclear membrane in sarcomeres and regulates sarcomere architecture.[8][9]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Desmin is a 53.5 kD protein composed of 470 amino acids, encoded by the human DES gene located on the long arm of chromosome 2.[10][11] There are three major domains to the desmin protein: a conserved alpha helix rod, a variable non alpha helix head, and a carboxy-terminal tail.[12] Desmin, as all intermediate filaments, shows no polarity when assembled.[12] The rod domain consists of 308 amino acids with parallel alpha helical coiled coil dimers and three linkers to disrupt it.[12] The rod domain connects to the head domain.<</A_RELEVANT>> The head domain 84 amino acids with many arginine, serine, and aromatic residues is important in filament assembly and dimer-dimer interactions.[12] The tail domain is responsible for the integration of filaments and interaction with proteins and organelles. <<A_RELEVANT>>Desmin is only expressed in vertebrates, however homologous proteins are found in many organisms.[12] Desmin is a subunit of intermediate filaments in cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle and smooth muscle tissue.[13] In cardiac muscle, desmin is present in Z-discs and intercalated discs.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Desmin has been shown to interact with desmoplakin[14] and αB-crystallin.[15]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Desmin was first described in 1976,[16] first purified in 1977,[17] the gene was cloned in 1989,[6] and the first knockout mouse was created in 1996.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>The function of desmin has been deduced through studies in knockout mice.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Desmin is one of the earliest protein markers for muscle tissue in embryogenesis as it is detected in the somites.[12][18] Although it is present early in the development of muscle cells, it is only expressed at low levels, and increases as the cell nears terminal differentiation.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>A similar protein, vimentin, is present in higher amounts during embryogenesis while desmin is present in higher amounts after differentiation.<</A_RELEVANT>> This suggests that there may be some interaction between the two in determining muscle cell differentiation. <<A_RELEVANT>>However desmin knockout mice develop normally and only experience defects later in life.[13] Since desmin is expressed at a low level during differentiation another protein may be able to compensate for desmin's function early in development but not later on.[19]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>In adult desmin-null mice, hearts from 10 week-old animals showed drastic alterations in muscle architecture, including a misalignment of myofibrils and disorganization and swelling of mitochondria; findings that were more severe in cardiac relative to skeletal muscle.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Cardiac tissue also exhibited progressive necrosis and calcification of the myocardium.[20] A separate study examined this in more detail in cardiac tissue and found that murine hearts lacking desmin developed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and chamber dilation combined with systolic dysfunction.[21] In adult muscle, desmin forms a scaffold around the Z-disk of the sarcomere and connects the Z-disk to the subsarcolemmal cytoskeleton.[22] It links the myofibrils laterally by connecting the Z-disks.[12] Through its connection to the sarcomere, desmin connects the contractile apparatus to the cell nucleus, mitochondria, and post-synaptic areas of motor endplates.[12] These connections maintain the structural and mechanical integrity of the cell during contraction while also helping in force transmission and longitudinal load bearing.[22][23]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>In human heart failure, desmin expression is upregulated, which has been hypothesized to be a defense mechanism in an attempt to maintain normal sarcomere alignment amidst disease pathogenesis.[24]  There is some evidence that desmin may also connect the sarcomere to the extracellular matrix (ECM) through desmosomes which could be important in signalling between the ECM and the sarcomere which could regulate muscle contraction and movement.[23] Finally, desmin may be important in mitochondria function.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>When desmin is not functioning properly there is improper mitochondrial distribution, number, morphology and function.[25][26] Since desmin links the mitochondria to the sarcomere it may transmit information about contractions and energy need and through this regulate the aerobic respiration rate of the muscle cell.<</A_RELEVANT>>

entity_document.title: Deoxyribose
entity_document.text:
Deoxyribose, or more precisely 2-deoxyribose, is a monosaccharide with idealized formula H−(C=O)−(CH2)−(CHOH)3−H. Its name indicates that it is a deoxy sugar, meaning that it is derived from the sugar ribose by loss of a hydroxy group. Discovered in 1929 by Phoebus Levene, deoxyribose is most notable for its presence in DNA. Since the pentose sugars arabinose and ribose only differ by the stereochemistry at C2′, 2-deoxyribose and 2-deoxyarabinose are equivalent, although the latter term is rarely used because ribose, not arabinose, is the precursor to deoxyribose.


== Structure ==
Several isomers exist with the formula H−(C=O)−(CH2)−(CHOH)3−H, but in deoxyribose all the hydroxyl groups are on the same side in the Fischer projection. The term "2-deoxyribose" may refer to either of two enantiomers: the biologically important d-2-deoxyribose and to the rarely encountered mirror image l-2-deoxyribose. d-2-deoxyribose is a precursor to the nucleic acid DNA. 2-deoxyribose is an aldopentose, that is, a monosaccharide with five carbon atoms and having an aldehyde functional group.
In aqueous solution, deoxyribose primarily exists as a mixture of three structures: the linear form H−(C=O)−(CH2)−(CHOH)3−H and two ring forms, deoxyribofuranose ("C3′-endo"), with a five-membered ring, and deoxyribopyranose ("C2′-endo"), with a six-membered ring. The latter form is predominant (whereas the C3′-endo form is favored for ribose). 


== Biological importance ==
As a component of DNA, 2-deoxyribose derivatives have an important role in biology. The DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) molecule, which is the main repository of genetic information in life, consists of a long chain of deoxyribose-containing units called nucleotides, linked via phosphate groups.  In the standard nucleic acid nomenclature, a DNA nucleotide consists of a deoxyribose molecule with an organic base (usually adenine, thymine, guanine or cytosine) attached to the 1′ ribose carbon.  The 5′ hydroxyl of each deoxyribose unit is replaced by a phosphate (forming a nucleotide) that is attached to the 3′ carbon of the deoxyribose in the preceding unit.  
The absence of the 2′ hydroxyl group in deoxyribose is apparently responsible for the increased mechanical flexibility of DNA compared to RNA, which allows it to assume the double-helix conformation, and also (in the eukaryotes) to be compactly coiled within the small cell nucleus.  The double-stranded DNA molecules are also typically much longer than RNA molecules. The backbone of RNA and DNA are structurally similar, but RNA is single stranded, and made from ribose as opposed to deoxyribose.
Other biologically important derivatives of deoxyribose include mono-, di-, and triphosphates, as well as 3′-5′ cyclic monophosphates.


=== Biosynthesis ===
Deoxyribose is generated from ribose 5-phosphate by enzymes called ribonucleotide reductases.  These enzymes catalyse the deoxygenation process.


=== Angiogenesis ===
In one study, deoxyribose was shown to have pro-angiogenic properties when applied topically in a gel to wounds in rats. In addition, this topical gel also increased Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF), which has been implicated in hair growth. This could potentially lead to future products to treat hair loss in humans.


== References ==

property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The Chinese name luo han guo means "arhat fruit".<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In Buddhism, an arhat is a monk who has attained enlightenment, also described as one who as attained the "fruition of arhatship" (Sanskrit: arhattaphala).[3] This was rendered in Chinese as luohanguo (lit. 'arhat fruit') which later became the Chinese and Western commercial designation for this type of sweet fruit.[4] It is called la hán quả in Vietnamese, which also means 'arhat fruit', or longevity fruit (also used for other fruits).[4]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The vine attains a length of 3 to 5 m (9.8 to 16 ft), climbing over other plants by means of tendrils which twine around anything they touch. The narrow, heart-shaped leaves are 10–20 cm (4–8 in) long. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The fruit is round or oblong, 4–8 cm (1.6–3.1 in) in diameter, smooth and yellow-brown in color.[10]  The inside of the fruit contains an edible pulp.<</Q_RELEVANT>> When dried, it forms a thin, light brown, brittle shell about 1 mm in thickness. The seeds are pale yellow and broadly ovate.[10]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Thus, the fruits are usually dried before further use and are sold in this fashion in Chinese herbal shops.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The fruits are dried slowly in ovens, preserving them and removing most of the unwanted aromas.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>However, this technique also leads to the formation of several bitter and astringent flavors.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This limits the use of the dried fruits and extracts to the preparation of diluted tea, soup, and as a sweetener for products that would usually have sugar or honey added to them.[11]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In this process, the peel and seeds are removed, and the pulped fruit is made into a fruit concentrate or puree.[12] Additional juice may be extracted from the remaining pulp with hot water.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The juice is homogenized, acidified slightly to prevent gelling and improve the flavor, then treated with pectinase or other enzymes to break down the pectin. Most of the off-flavor agents are then removed with ion-exchange resins, such as sulfonated polystyrene-divinylbenzene copolymer or polyacrylic acid. Alternatively, the off-flavors can be adsorbed by agents like charcoal or bentonite, which are removed by filtration; or precipitated with gelatin or other gelling agents. Most of the remaining sulfurous volatiles are then removed by low-pressure evaporation.[12] The juice is then pasteurized to inactivate remaining natural enzymes and kill microorganisms.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In Europe, it is classified as an unapproved novel food (not used in the food system before May 1997) which means that it may be marketed as a food or food ingredient only after a safety assessment and approval by the European Commission.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In 2019, the EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Flavourings (FAF) was asked by the European Commission to provide its scientific opinion on the safety of monkfruit extract as a food additive.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The panel concluded that the current body of research was insufficient.[15] As of 2023, Siraitia grosvenorii was not listed among approved Novel Foods in the EU.[16][17]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Siraitia grosvenorii, also known as monkfruit, luo han guo (Chinese: 羅漢果; pinyin: luóhàn guǒ), or Swingle fruit, is a herbaceous perennial vine of the gourd family, Cucurbitaceae.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It is native to southern China. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The plant is cultivated for its fruit extract containing mogrosides.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Mogroside extract has been used as a low-calorie sugar substitute for drinks and in traditional Chinese medicine. One mogroside, mogroside V, creates a sweetness sensation 250 times stronger than sucrose.[2]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>One analysis of 200 candidate genes of Siraitia grosvenorii revealed five enzyme families involved in the synthesis of mogroside V: squalene epoxidases, triterpenoid synthases, epoxide hydrolases, cytochrome P450s, and UDP-glucosyltransferases.[2] The metabolic pathway for mogroside biosynthesis involves an initial stage of fruit development when squalene is metabolized to di-glucosylated, tetra-hydroxycucurbitadienols, then during fruit maturation, branched glucosyl groups are added and catalyzed, leading to the sweet M4, M5, and M6 mogrosides.[2]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Monkfruit was first mentioned in the records of 13th-century Chinese monks in Guangxi in the region of Guilin.[3] The difficulty of cultivation meant the fruit did not become part of the Chinese herbal tradition which depended on more readily available products.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The interior fruit is eaten fresh, and the rind is used to make tea.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The monkfruit is notable for its sweetness, which can be concentrated from its juice.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The fruit contains 25–38% of various carbohydrates, mainly fructose and glucose.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The sweetness of the fruit is increased by the mogrosides, a group of triterpene glycosides (saponins).<</Q_RELEVANT>> The five different mogrosides are numbered from I to V; the main component is mogroside V, which is also known as esgoside.[3]

property_documents.title: Beta vulgaris
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The species description of Beta vulgaris was made in 1753 by Carl Linnaeus in Species Plantarum, at the same time creating the genus Beta.[7] Linnaeus regarded sea beet, chard and red beet as varieties (at that time, sugar beet and mangelwurzel had not been selected yet).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>In the second edition of Species Plantarum (1762), Linnaeus separated the sea beet as its own species, Beta maritima, and left only the cultivated beets in Beta vulgaris.[8] Today sea beet and cultivated beets are considered as belonging to the same species, because they may hybridize and form fertile offspring.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The taxonomy of the various cultivated races has a long and complicated history, they were treated at the rank of either subspecies, or convarieties or varieties.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Now rankless cultivar groups are used, according to the International Code of Nomenclature for Cultivated Plants.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Roman and Jewish literary sources suggest that in the 1st century BC the domestic beet was represented in the Mediterranean basin primarily by leafy forms like chard and spinach beet.[29] Zohary and Hopf also argue that it is very probable that beetroot cultivars were also grown at the time, and some Roman recipes support this.[29][30] Later English and German sources show that beetroots were commonly cultivated in Medieval Europe.[30]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris (Syn.: Beta vulgaris subsp. cicla (L.) Arcang., Beta vulgaris subsp. rapacea (Koch) Döll).: all cultivated beets belong to this subspecies.[9][2][10] There are five cultivar groups:<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Modern sugar beets date back to mid-18th century Silesia where the king of Prussia subsidised experiments aimed at processes for sugar extraction.[30][32] In 1747 Andreas Marggraf isolated sugar from beetroots and found them at concentrations of 1.3-1.6%.[13] He also demonstrated that sugar could be extracted from beets that was the same as that produced from sugarcane.[32] His student, Franz Karl Achard, evaluated 23 varieties of mangelwurzel for sugar content and selected a local race from Halberstadt in modern-day Saxony-Anhalt, Germany.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Moritz Baron von Koppy and his son further selected from this race for white, conical tubers.[13] The selection was named 'Weiße Schlesische Zuckerrübe', meaning white Silesian sugar beet, and boasted about a 6% sugar content.[13][30] This selection is the progenitor of all modern sugar beets.[13]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Cicla Group,[12] spinach beet or chard (Syn.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>B. v. subsp. vulgaris convar. cicla var. cicla)[13] - The leaf beet group has a long history dating to the second millennium BC.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The first cultivated forms were believed to have been domesticated in the Mediterranean, but were introduced to the Middle East, India, and finally China by 850 AD. <<Q_RELEVANT>>These were used as medicinal plants in Ancient Greece and Medieval Europe.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Their popularity declined in Europe following the introduction of spinach. <<Q_RELEVANT>>This variety is widely cultivated for its leaves, which are usually cooked like spinach.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It can be found in many grocery stores around the world.

Crassa Group,[12] mangelwurzel (Syn. <<Q_RELEVANT>>B. v. subsp. v. convar. vulgaris var. crassa)[13] - This variety was developed in the 18th century from the garden beet for its tubers for use as a fodder crop.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Cicla Group,[12] spinach beet or chard (Syn.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>B. v. subsp. vulgaris convar. cicla var. cicla)[13] - The leaf beet group has a long history dating to the second millennium BC.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The first cultivated forms were believed to have been domesticated in the Mediterranean, but were introduced to the Middle East, India, and finally China by 850 AD. <<Q_RELEVANT>>These were used as medicinal plants in Ancient Greece and Medieval Europe.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Their popularity declined in Europe following the introduction of spinach. <<Q_RELEVANT>>This variety is widely cultivated for its leaves, which are usually cooked like spinach.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It can be found in many grocery stores around the world.

Crassa Group,[12] mangelwurzel (Syn. <<Q_RELEVANT>>B. v. subsp. v. convar. vulgaris var. crassa)[13] - This variety was developed in the 18th century from the garden beet for its tubers for use as a fodder crop.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The color of red/purple beetroot is due to a variety of betalain pigments, unlike most other red plants, such as red cabbage, which contain anthocyanin pigments.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The composition of different betalain pigments can vary, resulting in strains of beetroot which are yellow or other colors in addition to the familiar deep red.[19] Some of the betalains in beets are betanin, isobetanin, probetanin, and neobetanin (the red to violet ones are known collectively as betacyanin).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Other pigments contained in beet are indicaxanthin and vulgaxanthins (yellow to orange pigments known as betaxanthins).<</Q_RELEVANT>> Indicaxanthin has been shown as a powerful protective antioxidant for thalassemia and prevents the breakdown of alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E).[citation needed]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Betacyanin in beetroot may cause red urine in people who are unable to break it down.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This is called beeturia.[20]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

property_documents.title: Pleurotus ostreatus
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The cap is broad, fan or oyster-shaped, and 2–30 centimetres (1–12 inches) wide.[5] In the wild, it ranges from white to gray or brown; the margin is inrolled when young, smooth and often somewhat lobed or wavy.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The flesh is white, firm, and varies in thickness due to stipe arrangement.<</Q_RELEVANT>> The stipe, if present, is up to 4 cm (1+1⁄2 in) long and thick,[2] off-center and attaching laterally to wood. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The gills are whitish, sometimes becoming yellowish, and decurrent if a stalk is present.[2] The spore print is white to lilac-gray, and best viewed on a dark background.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The mushroom has the bittersweet aroma of benzaldehyde or bitter almonds.[6]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Both the Latin and common names refer to the shape of the fruiting body.[4] The Latin pleurotus (side-ear) refers to the sideways growth of the stem with respect to the cap, while the Latin ostreatus (and the English common name, oyster) refers to the shape of the cap which resembles the bivalve of the same name.[4] The oyster reference may also derive from the slippery texture of the mushroom.[4]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Commercial cultivation of this mushroom first began in Germany as a subsistence measure during World War I,[15] and it is now grown commercially around the world for food.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>While this mushroom is often seen growing on dying hardwood trees, it only appears to be acting saprophytically, rather than parasitically.<</Q_RELEVANT>> As the tree dies of other causes, P. ostreatus grows on the rapidly increasing mass of dead and dying wood. <<Q_RELEVANT>>They actually benefit the forest by decomposing the dead wood, returning vital elements and minerals to the ecosystem in a form usable to other plants and organisms.[4] Additionally, oyster mushrooms bioaccumulate lithium.[12]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Pleurotus ostreatus, commonly known as the oyster mushroom,[2] grey oyster mushroom,[3] oyster fungus, hiratake, or pearl oyster mushroom, is a popular edible mushroom found in temperate and subtropical forests around the world.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>It is related to the similarly cultivated Pleurotus eryngii (king oyster mushroom).[citation needed] Other similar species include P. columbinus, P. cornucopiae,[2] Hohenbuehelia petaloides, the hairy-capped Phyllotopsis nidulans, and the smaller Pleurocybella porrigens.[7]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Omphalotus nidiformis is a toxic lookalike found in Australia. <<Q_RELEVANT>>In North America, potential lookalikes include the toxic muscarine-containing O. olivascens (the western jack-o'-lantern mushroom) and Clitocybe dealbata (the ivory funnel mushroom).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Some toxic Lentinellus species are similar in appearance, but have gills with jagged edges and finely haired caps.[8]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The oyster mushroom is widespread in many temperate and subtropical forests throughout the world, although it is absent from the Pacific Northwest of North America, being replaced by P. pulmonarius and P. populinus.[9] It is a saprotroph that acts as a primary decomposer of wood, especially deciduous trees, and beech trees in particular.[10] It is a white-rot wood-decay fungus.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The oyster mushroom can be found in many habitats, year round in the United Kingdom, while some related species (e.g. the branched oyster mushroom) grow only on trees.[11]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The oyster mushroom is a choice edible.[5] Oyster mushrooms are used in Czech, Polish, and Slovak contemporary cuisine in soups and stews in a similar fashion to meat, as well as breaded to become a vegetarian alternative to the kotlet in Polish dishes.[16][17] It is a delicacy in Japanese, Korean and Chinese cuisine.[citation needed] In Indonesia it is common to find street food vendors selling crispy deep fried oyster mushrooms.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It is frequently served on its own, in soups, stuffed, or in stir-fry recipes with soy sauce. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Oyster mushrooms may be used in sauces, such as vegetarian oyster sauce.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The mushroom's taste has been described as mild with a slight odor similar to anise.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It is best when picked young; as the mushroom ages, the flesh becomes tough and the flavor becomes acrid.[18]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Spahr, D.L. (2009). <<Q_RELEVANT>>Edible and Medicinal Mushrooms of New England and Eastern Canada.<</Q_RELEVANT>> North Atlantic Books. ISBN 978-1-55643-795-3.

<<Q_RELEVANT>>All major lineages of the oyster mushroom are carnivorous.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The mushroom's mycelia can kill and digest nematodes, which is believed to be a way in which the mushroom obtains nitrogen.[13] P. ostreatus is one of at least 700 known nematophagous mushrooms.[14]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The pearl oyster mushroom is also used to create mycelium bricks, mycelium furniture, and leather-like products.[citation needed]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Oyster mushrooms can also be used industrially for mycoremediation purposes.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Oyster mushrooms were used to treat soil that had been polluted with diesel oil.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The mushroom was able to convert 95% of the oil into non-toxic compounds.[19] P. ostreatus is also capable of growing upon and degrading oxo-biodegradable plastic bags;[20] it can also contribute to the degradation of renewable polyethylene.[21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

Lincoff, G.H. (1981). <<Q_RELEVANT>>National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Mushrooms.<</Q_RELEVANT>> Knopf. ISBN 978-0-394-51992-0.

property_documents.title: Pleurotus
property_documents.document:
<<Q_RELEVANT>>The crew of the Fram2 orbital mission are planning to grow oyster mushrooms in space for the first time.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>The code name for this experiment is Mission MushVroom, and is led by FOODiQ Global, an Australian company.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>If successful, these mushrooms could provide a sustainable food source during lengthy space missions.[24]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The classification of species within the genus Pleurotus is difficult due to high phenotypic variability across wide geographic ranges, geographic overlap of species, and ongoing evolution and speciation.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Early taxonomic efforts placed the oyster mushrooms within a very broad Agaricus as Agaricus ostreatus (Jacq. 1774).<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Paul Kummer defined the genus Pleurotus in 1871; since then, the genus has been narrowed with some species reclassified to other genera, such as Favolaschia, Hohenbuehelia, Lentinus, Marasmiellus, Omphalotus, Panellus, Pleurocybella, and Resupinatus.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>See Singer (1986)[4] for an example of Pleurotus taxonomy based on morphological characteristics.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>More recently, molecular phylogenetics has been utilized to determine genetic and evolutionary relationships between groups within the genus, delineating discrete clades.[5][6][7] Pleurotus, along with the closely related genus Hohenbuehelia, has been shown to be monophyletic.[8]  Tests of cross-breeding viability between groups have been used to further define which groups are deserving of species rank, as opposed to subspecies, variety, or synonymy.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>If two groups of morphologically distinct Pleurotus fungi are able to cross-breed and produce fertile offspring, they meet one definition of species.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>These reproductively discrete groups, referred to as intersterility groups, have begun to be defined in Pleurotus.[6][9]  Many binomial names used in literature are now being grouped together as species complexes using this technique, and may change.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The following species list is organized according to 1. phylogenetic clade,[5][7] 2. intersterility group (group number in Roman numerals) or sub-clade,[6][9] and then 3. any older binomial names that have been found to be closely related, reproductively compatible, or synonymous, although they may no longer be taxonomically valid.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>This list is likely to be incomplete.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Oyster mushrooms are some of the most commonly cultivated edible mushrooms.[18] They are prepared by being torn up or sliced, especially in stir fry or sauté, because they are consistently thin, and so will cook more evenly than uncut mushrooms of other types.[22] They are often used in vegetarian cuisine.[23]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

The caps may be laterally attached (with no stipe). If there is a stipe, it is normally eccentric and the gills are decurrent along it. <<Q_RELEVANT>>The term pleurotoid is used for any mushroom with this general shape.[1]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>Pleurotus is a genus of gilled mushrooms with species known as oyster, abalone, or tree mushrooms.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>It includes some of the most commonly cultivated edible mushrooms in the world, such as P. ostreatus.<</Q_RELEVANT>> <<Q_RELEVANT>>Additionally, some species have been used in the mycoremediation of pollutants.<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>In addition to being saprotrophic, all species of Pleurotus are also nematophagous, catching nematodes by paralyzing them with a toxin.[20][8] In the case of the carnivorous mushroom Pleurotus ostreatus, it was shown that small, fragile lollipop-shaped structures (toxocysts) on fungal hyphae contain a volatile ketone, 3-octanone, which disrupts the cell membrane integrity of nematodes, leading to rapid cell and organismal death, hypothetically either to defend themselves and/or to acquire nutrients.[21]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The spores are smooth and elongated (described as "cylindrical").<</Q_RELEVANT>> Where hyphae meet, they are joined by clamp connections. <<Q_RELEVANT>>Pleurotus is not considered to be a bracket fungus, and most of the species are monomitic (with a soft consistency).<</Q_RELEVANT>> However, remarkably, P. dryinus can sometimes be dimitic, meaning that it has additional skeletal hyphae, which give it a tougher consistency like bracket fungi.[2]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The genus name Pleurotus refers to the mushroom caps being laterally attached to the substrate.<</Q_RELEVANT>> It is derived of the Ancient Greek word πλευρόν: pleurón rib, side.[17]

<<Q_RELEVANT>>The 2007 Cosco Busan oil spill was remediated partly by using 1,000 mats of human hair collected from Bay Area salons woven into mats, then used to grow oyster mushrooms, helping to absorb the oil.[26]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>After the 2017 Tubbs Fire in California, oyster mushrooms were grown to help remediate toxic ash run-off.[27]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

I. <<Q_RELEVANT>>P. ostreatus (oyster or pearl oyster mushroom) – North America and northern Eurasia[6]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

II. <<Q_RELEVANT>>P. pulmonarius (phoenix or Indian oyster mushroom) – North America, Eurasia, and Australasia[7][10]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

VI. <<Q_RELEVANT>>P. eryngii (king oyster mushroom) – Europe and the Middle East[6]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

IV. <<Q_RELEVANT>>P. cornucopiae (branched oyster mushroom) – Europe<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>P. citrinopileatus (golden oyster mushroom) – eastern Asia<</Q_RELEVANT>>

<<Q_RELEVANT>>P. euosmus (tarragon oyster mushroom)<</Q_RELEVANT>>

V. <<Q_RELEVANT>>P. djamor (pink oyster mushroom) – pantropical<</Q_RELEVANT>>

VII. <<Q_RELEVANT>>P. cystidiosus (abalone mushroom) – global<</Q_RELEVANT>>

X. <<Q_RELEVANT>>P. tuber-regium (king tuber mushroom) – Africa, Asia, Australasia[14][7]<</Q_RELEVANT>>

question: The first compound is a toxic alkaloid that originates from the castor plant, can serve as a biomarker of ricin poisoning, and is known to sublimate between 170 °C and 180 °C at 20 mmHg. The second compound is an oral medication used to prevent gout attacks, is also employed in the management of pericarditis, and its injectable form is considered toxic. Using reliable chemical databases, determine how many times heavier the second compound is than the first compound by comparing their molecular weights.

property_documents.title: Colchicine
property_documents.document:
<<A_RELEVANT>>Colchicine is a medication used to prevent and treat gout,[3][4] to treat familial Mediterranean fever[5] and Behçet's disease,[6] and to reduce the risk of myocardial infarction.[7] The American College of Rheumatology recommends colchicine, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or steroids in the treatment of gout.[8][9] Other uses for colchicine include the management of pericarditis.[10]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Colchicine is taken by mouth.[11] The injectable route of administration for colchicine can be toxic.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>In 2008, the US Food and Drug Administration removed all injectable colchicine from the US market.[12][13]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic index, so overdosing is a significant risk.<</A_RELEVANT>> <<A_RELEVANT>>Common side effects of colchicine include gastrointestinal upset, particularly at high doses.[14] Severe side effects may include pancytopenia (low blood cell counts) and rhabdomyolysis (damage to skeletal muscle), and the medication can be deadly in overdose.[11] Whether colchicine is safe for use during pregnancy is unclear, but its use during breastfeeding appears to be safe.[11][15] Colchicine works by decreasing inflammation via multiple mechanisms.[16]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Colchicine, in the form of autumn crocus (Colchicum autumnale) crude extract, was used as early as 1500 BC to treat joint swelling.[17] It was approved for medical use in the United States in 1961.[2] It is available as a generic medication.[15] In 2023, it was the 215th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 2 million prescriptions.[18][19]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Colchicine is used in plant breeding to induce polyploidy, in which the number of chromosomes in plant cells are doubled.<</A_RELEVANT>> This helps produce larger, hardier, faster-growing, and in general, more desirable plants than the normally diploid parents.[20]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Colchicine is an alternative for those unable to tolerate nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) when treating gout.[21][22][23][24] Low doses (1.2 mg in one hour, followed by 0.6 mg an hour later) appear to be well tolerated and may reduce gout symptoms and pain, perhaps as effectively as NSAIDs.[25] At higher doses, side effects (primarily diarrhea, nausea, or vomiting) limit its use.[25]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>For treating gout symptoms, colchicine is taken orally, with or without food, as symptoms first appear.[26] Subsequent doses may be needed if symptoms worsen.[26]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>There is preliminary evidence that daily colchicine may be effective as a long-term prophylaxis when used with allopurinol to reduce the risk of increased uric acid levels and acute gout flares;[27] adverse gastrointestinal effects may occur,[28] though overall the risk of serious side effects is low.[29][30]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>In June 2023, the US FDA approved a low-dose regimen of colchicine (brand name Lodoco) to reduce the risk of further disorders in adults with existing cardiovascular diseases.[31][32] As an anti-inflammatory drug, Lodoco in a dose of 0.5 mg per day reduced the rate of cardiovascular events by 31% in people with established atherosclerosis and by 23% in people with recent myocardial infarction.[32] Colchicine was most effective in combination therapy with lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory medications.[32] The mechanism for this effect of colchicine is unknown.[31]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Colchicine is also used as an anti-inflammatory agent for long-term treatment of Behçet's disease.[33] It appears to have limited effect in relapsing polychondritis, as it may only be useful for the treatment of chondritis and mild skin symptoms.[34] It is a component of therapy for several other conditions, including pericarditis, pulmonary fibrosis, biliary cirrhosis, various vasculitides, pseudogout, spondyloarthropathy, calcinosis, scleroderma, and amyloidosis.[33][35][36]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Research regarding the efficacy of colchicine in many of these diseases has not been performed.[36] It is also used in the treatment of familial Mediterranean fever,[33] in which it reduces attacks and the long-term risk of amyloidosis.[37]<</A_RELEVANT>>

<<A_RELEVANT>>Colchicine is effective for prevention of atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery.[38] In people with recent myocardial infarction (recent heart attack), it has been found to reduce risk of future cardiovascular events.<</A_RELEVANT>> Its clinical use may grow to include this indication.[39][40]

<<A_RELEVANT>>Long-term (prophylactic) regimens of oral colchicine are absolutely contraindicated in people with advanced kidney failure (including those on dialysis).[26] About 10–20% of a colchicine dose is excreted unchanged by the kidneys; it is not removed by hemodialysis.<</A_RELEVANT>> Cumulative toxicity is a high probability in this clinical setting, and a severe neuromyopathy may result. The presentation includes a progressive onset of proximal weakness, elevated creatine kinase, and sensorimotor polyneuropathy. <<A_RELEVANT>>Colchicine toxicity can be potentiated by the concomitant use of cholesterol-lowering drugs.[26]<</A_RELEVANT>>
